# derek

58. Warehouse supervisor at a haulage depot, Coventry. Type 2 diabetes,
managed on metformin, diagnosed a few years before this record starts.
Married to Pam. Two adult kids, both moved out. Synthetic; any resemblance
to a real person is accidental and unintended.

## In his own words

He would not put it this way, because he would not put it any way at all -
he is not a man who journals about himself. What the record actually holds
is four months of a prescribed evening walk, done three times a week,
logged by whatever his phone happens to catch, and a handful of lines typed
in the evening that say less than what happened.

"Bit of indigestion on the hill again" is the whole of what he is willing
to write down. Five times between April and June, going up the incline on
the hill loop, something happens that slows him right down for the best
part of ten minutes. He calls it heartburn, indigestion, a dodgy stomach.
Once, in the middle of June, it went up into his jaw. He sat on the wall,
it passed, he finished the walk, and he told nobody that evening - the
one line about it went into the record the next day, described as already
over.

## The record his life produces

- Four months: 2030-03-01 to 2030-06-30. Low density throughout; he does
  not go looking for reasons to open the app.
- Weight: fourteen rows off a plain dial scale at home, weekly-ish. Three
  of the fourteen were typed by Pam from what he called out to her, and
  each of those three is about 2 kg lighter than the scale actually showed.
- Sessions: fifty walks, phone-app vendor-classified, pace and duration
  only - no heart rate, no calories, nothing else. Thirty-five on the
  prescribed hill loop, fifteen on the flat alternative he reaches for more
  often in the weeks right after a bad one.
- Journal: five short notes, all about the hill loop, all short of the
  word that would actually describe what is happening.
- Medical: one standing row for the metformin, self-reported, unremarkable.
- Context: one row for a week in a caravan in Wales, no walks logged.
- Daily: six mundane notes across four months. No steps, ever - he has no
  wearable, and his phone stays in a locker for most of an eight-to-ten
  hour shift on his feet.

## The axis he stresses

A real, recurring cardiac symptom that is never once named as such,
anywhere in the record, by design - minimised in prose while the numbers
underneath tell a straighter story. A wife who sometimes logs for him,
carrying his own rounding-down along with her handwriting. A job that
makes him more active than the record can ever show. This is the sharpest
test of the medical boundary in the corpus: the record must be readable as
what it is without the engine ever crossing into diagnosis, care
instruction, or false reassurance.
